title: Oil India Hits Gas Twice in the Andaman Sea. India's Most Promising Frontier Basin Just Got Real.
excerpt: Two successful wells out of three in less than nine months. With the Strait of Hormuz half-shut and oil at $97, the timing could not be more pointed.
body:
Oil India Limited has struck natural gas for a second time in the Andaman Sea, confirming the frontier basin's potential as a meaningful domestic energy source — and delivering the news at a moment when India desperately needs one.

The discovery at the Sri Vijayapuram-3 exploratory well, about 15 kilometres off the east coast of the Andaman Islands at a water depth of 355 metres, follows a successful find at Vijayapuram-2 in September 2025. Two out of three wells in the current campaign have now confirmed hydrocarbons, a hit rate that deepwater geologists consider remarkably encouraging for a basin that was, until recently, barely explored.

Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri announced the find on X, calling it evidence of "an ocean of energy opportunities" in the Andaman Sea.

## What They Found

Initial production testing at a depth of over 1,900 metres in the Eocene formation established the presence of natural gas through continuous flaring — meaning the reservoir produced gas immediately after perforation, with sustained pressure indicating a productive formation. Oil India is now sampling the gas to assess its composition, calorific value, and isotope genesis, the technical steps that determine whether a discovery is commercially viable or merely geologically interesting.

The well sits in the AN-OSHP-2018/1 block, acquired by Oil India under the government's Open Acreage Licensing Policy. After the first discovery, the company completed reprocessing of existing 2D seismic data and acquired 600 square kilometres of fresh 3D seismic data to map the basin more precisely. Appraisal drilling — the stage that tests whether gas volumes justify development infrastructure — is expected to begin once that interpretation work is complete.

## Why It Matters Now

The strategic context transforms what might otherwise be a routine exploration update into a story with national implications.

India sourced more than 40 percent of its crude imports and roughly 90 percent of its liquefied petroleum gas through the Strait of Hormuz before the Iran war disrupted the passage. Brent crude crossed $97 a barrel on Monday. State fuel retailers have raised prices four times since mid-May. The rupee is under record pressure. The RBI has just deployed a $50 billion FCNR scheme to attract foreign exchange.

Against that backdrop, any credible domestic energy source matters. The Andaman Basin is not going to replace Persian Gulf imports overnight — gas fields take years to develop, and the region's deep waters present formidable engineering challenges. But back-to-back discoveries validate the basin's geological promise and, crucially, justify the kind of sustained investment that turns promise into production.

## The Samudra Manthan Mission

The Andaman campaign falls under the Samudra Manthan Mission, a national deep-water exploration push announced by Prime Minister Modi on Independence Day 2025. The programme envisions a large number of deepwater and ultra-deepwater wells across India's offshore basins, with collaborations from global majors including Petrobras, TotalEnergies, BP, Shell, and ExxonMobil.

Puri noted that the Andaman discoveries will help advance exploration in coordination with these partners — a signal that India may seek joint ventures to accelerate appraisal and development, given the capital intensity of offshore gas projects.

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs watching from the US, UK, and the Gulf, the Andaman story intersects with the oil-price crisis that is already reshaping their remittance economics. A weaker rupee means remittances buy more at home, but it also signals macroeconomic fragility. Domestic gas production, even years down the line, would reduce India's import bill, stabilise the currency, and lower the household energy costs that have made the front pages this month.

The Andaman Sea may be a long way from producing commercial gas. But for the first time, the geology is cooperating — and India's need has never been more urgent.
